summary: This note is a Wikipedia-derived excerpt on Alexander Graham Bell's family background, early life, and public legacy. It covers his family's long association with elocution through his grandfather, uncle, and father, including his father's book The Standard Elocutionist and Bell's training in Visible Speech. It also describes commemorations of his 150th birth anniversary in 1997 on Royal Bank of Scotland banknotes and Canadian coins, his nationality status, and an early note on his harmonic telegraph experiments in Brantford.
one_line: Overview of Alexander Graham Bell's elocutionist family, his Visible Speech training, commemorations of his legacy, and his citizenship status.
key_facts: The Bell family home was in Cambridge, Massachusetts, until 1880, when Bell's father-in-law bought a house in Washington, D.C.
In 1882 a home in Washington, D.C. was bought for Bell's family so they could be with him during patent dispute court cases.
Bell's grandfather, Alexander Bell, in London, his uncle in Dublin, and his father in Edinburgh were all elocutionists.
Bell's father published The Standard Elocutionist (1860), which appeared in Edinburgh in 1868.
The Standard Elocutionist appeared in 168 British editions and sold over a quarter of a million copies in the United States alone.
Bell's father taught him and his brothers to write Visible Speech and to identify any symbol and its accompanying sound.
Bell could decipher Visible Speech representing virtually every language, including Latin, Scottish Gaelic, and Sanskrit, without prior knowledge of their pronunciation.
The Royal Bank of Scotland issued a special series of commemorative £1 banknotes in 1997 to mark the 150th anniversary of Bell's birth.
The Government of Canada honored Bell in 1997 with a C$100 gold coin for the 150th anniversary of his birth.
The Government of Canada issued a silver dollar coin in 2009 in honor of the 100th anniversary of flight in Canada.
The first flight in Canada was made by the Silver Dart, an airplane designed under Bell's tutelage.
Bell was a British subject in his early life in Scotland and later in Canada until 1882, when he became a naturalized citizen of the United States.
In 1915, Bell said: "I am not one of those hyphenated Americans who claim allegiance to two countries."
Bell returned to Brantford after six months abroad and continued experiments with his "harmonic telegraph".
The harmonic telegraph concept was that messages could be sent through a single wire if each message was transmitted at a different pitch.
